statement: One writer publishes (k, 7k) for increasing k while readers call try_read concurrently. A successful read returns a pair that was actually written (never torn), not older than what the reader is guaranteed to see, never going backwards for the same reader; try_read may fail while a write overlaps. Run alone, reads succeed and see the latest write. No data race — the payload must be atomic (relaxed is fine); the classic plain-memory seqlock is undefined behaviour in C++ and is rejected. Premise: fewer than 2^(BITS-1) writes overlap one read (otherwise the counter wraps to the same value and no seqlock can tell).
contract: template<unsigned BITS> struct SeqLock { void write(int a, int b); bool try_read(int& a, int& b); };  single writer; the sequence counter must wrap at 2^BITS (BITS = 32 in production, shrunk for verification); initial payload (0, 0).
instantiate: template struct SeqLock<3>; template struct SeqLock<32>;
scenario_rule: at least one scenario with two readers, one with a reader that reads twice, and one shrunk scenario whose concurrent writes cross the counter wrap-around (3-bit counter pushed to 6 by solo writes, then 6 -> 7 -> 0 -> 1 -> 2)

survivor_annotations.why: a seqlock only needs the counter to be odd while a write is in progress and to differ from its previous value afterwards; stepping to s-1 instead of s+1 for the odd in-progress value is just as valid. Modulo 2^BITS the values stay distinct and the parity is unchanged, so the wrap-around period is the same

a seqlock only needs the counter to be odd while a write is in progress and to differ from its previous value afterwards; stepping to s-2 instead of s+2 for the final even value is just as valid (the counter counts down). Modulo 2^BITS the values stay distinct and the parity is unchanged, so the wrap-around period is the same
